body: Maximum peak-to-trough fall inside each winner's own up-move (weekly closes), 27 windows: median −41%; 22 of 27 (81%) had at least one ≥30% drawdown, and 14 (52%) at least one ≥40%. Examples: Bajaj Finance −61% (2020), Tata Elxsi −59% (2018–20), APL Apollo −57% (2018–19), BSE −55% (2022–23), Dixon −52% (2021–23), Page −52% (2018–20), Avanti −51% (2012–13), Balkrishna −48%, HAL −47% (2020), Caplin −47% (2013), Polycab −45%, CDSL −44%. The shallowest were Pidilite (−26%), Eicher 2008–17 (−26%), Trent 2020–24 (−22%) and Kaynes (−20%, a short run). Most of these drawdowns came from market shocks (2013 taper, 2018 small-cap crash, 2020 COVID) or de-rating while EPS kept rising (Caplin 2017–20: EPS 2x, price −68%), not from broken theses. Holding rule: a ≥40% fall is the normal cost of a multibagger. The question at −40% is whether EPS and ROCE are intact (hold or add) or the driver has broken (exit). Position size so a −60% move is survivable. Extends insight:winners-drawdowns to India.
title: Median in-run drawdown of Indian multibaggers −41%; 22 of 27 fell ≥30% on the way up

body: RULE: our disqualifier (pledge >25% of promoter holding or rising) stays the DEFAULT; an override must be written down as a decision record. Grade severity on six questions: (1) PURPOSE: disclosed and specific (family debt from a known investment, funding the listed company's own rights issue) vs undisclosed or to fund other group companies; (2) SIZE: % of promoter holding and % of total equity, plus the price cushion before margin calls; (3) TREND: falling via actual stake sales or repayments (Apollo Hospitals: ~76% in 2019 -> ~2% by Aug 2025 after block sales) vs rising while price rises (Zee/Essel 59% -> ~90%); (4) LENDER: banks with long tenor vs NBFCs/MFs with loan-against-shares and short tenor (2018-19 IL&FS freeze turned MF pledges into fire sales); (5) LISTED-COMPANY LEVERAGE: is the company itself unlevered and cash-generative, or does it also guarantee group debt; (6) GROUP HISTORY: any past invocations, diversion or contagion (ADAG, Essel, Future, Cox & Kings = severe). A pledge that is high but falling, disclosed, bank-funded, at the family level, in a clean group with an unlevered company is a sizing and monitoring issue; a rising pledge with undisclosed purpose in a group with a history is a disqualifier. Also treat non-disposal undertakings and 'encumbrances' as pledges. HONEST CAVEAT: even benign pledges are reflexive in a crash; Apollo worked partly because the price rose. Size such positions small and track quarterly SAST disclosures.

data.override_needs: all six checks pass + decision record + small size

title: Grading a promoter pledge: purpose, size, trend, lender, leverage, group history

body: Womack, 'Do Brokerage Analysts' Recommendations Have Investment Value?' (Journal of Finance 51(1), 1996; ~1,900 citations), 14 large US brokers 1989-91: new buy recommendations saw about +3% in the 3-day window, with mean drift of about +2.4% over the next month. New sells (rarer and costlier for the analyst) saw about -4.7% at the announcement and drift of about -9% over six months. Sell calls carry more information than buys. Barber, Lehavy, McNichols and Trueman, 'Can Investors Profit from the Prophets?' (Journal of Finance 56(2), 2001; ~870 citations), consensus recommendations 1985-96: buying the most highly rated stocks and shorting the least favourable earned over 4% a year in gross abnormal returns, but the strategy needed very high turnover. After realistic costs the abnormal returns were not reliably different from zero, and the edge required daily rebalancing. Replicated: yes; Jegadeesh et al. (2004) find that changes and revisions are more informative than levels. Use for us: (1) recommendation LEVELS are noise; the rare downgrade to sell from a respected analyst, or a sharp estimate revision, is the informative event; (2) the residual value of research is in the analyst's facts and channel checks, not their rating; (3) in India, sell ratings are rare, so a broker initiating with a 'reduce' on a promoter-favoured stock is a strong signal to investigate.
title: Analyst recommendations carry information (Womack 1996) but gross alpha is eaten by turnover (Barber-Lehavy-McNichols-Trueman 2001)

body: Across this literature sweep, the most consistent result is that prices underreact to information that is public but costly to process. Lazy Prices (Cohen-Malloy-Nguyen 2020): filing text changes predicted returns for up to 18 months, with no announcement reaction (insight:lazy-prices-filing-changes). PEAD (Bernard-Thomas 1989): earnings surprises drift for 60+ days, more in small and under-covered firms. Friday and busy-day news (DellaVigna-Pollet, Hirshleifer-Lim-Teoh 2009): drift is around 70% larger when attention is low. Customer-supplier links (Cohen-Frazzini 2008): about 1.5% a month when few investors hold both firms. Frog in the pan (Da-Gurun-Warachka 2014): gradual information is underweighted. Effect sizes decay in US large caps once machines read the data (Martineau 2022 on PEAD; McLean-Pontiff decay). The common mechanism is limited attention plus processing cost, which is exactly what an individual with patience and structured note-taking can supply for a small universe, while quant funds avoid it for capacity reasons. Implications for FEIN: (1) our edge should be reading what others skip in Indian small and mid caps (AR diffs, CARO notes, related-party notes, concall Q&A, customer disclosures, exchange pledge/PIT feeds), not trading speed; (2) the edge is strongest where coverage is thinnest, but so is governance risk, so pair every 'under-followed' signal with the disqualifier checklist; (3) measure the drift ourselves on our own records before trusting it.
title: Synthesis: an 'inattention premium' runs through Lazy Prices, PEAD, Friday/distraction and supplier-link studies
